analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax on very large inherited estates from 40% to 20%.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the estate tax rate nearly in half was introduced in the Senate in 2021, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top federal estate tax rate — the tax on money and property passed on after death, which only applies to very large estates — from 40% down to 20%. It would apply to estates of people dying after 2020. It also exempts the resulting revenue loss from the budget rules that normally require tax cuts to be paid for. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and beneficiaries of the largest estates — the tax applies only to inherited wealth above a high exemption threshold, so a rate cut from 40% to 20% almost entirely benefits the wealthiest families and dynastic wealth holders.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the top rate on estates, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers from 40% to 20%, halving the tax owed on the largest inherited fortunes.
Exempts the bill's revenue loss from both statutory PAYGO scorecards and the Senate PAYGO scorecard, so the cut would not have to be offset by other tax increases or spending cuts.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury absorbs the lost revenue, and ultimately taxpayers and users of federal services bear that cost; no offsetting revenue is provided, since the bill exempts itself from pay-as-you-go rules.

drawbacks.text: The tax cut is unoffset — the bill expressly exempts its budgetary effects from PAYGO rules, so it adds to deficits rather than being paid for.
Because the estate tax reaches only the largest inherited fortunes, the benefit is concentrated among the wealthiest households rather than spread broadly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, targeted tax cut to the heirs of very large estates while adding to deficits, since it exempts itself from the rules requiring tax cuts to be paid for. The cost is spread across all taxpayers; the benefit is concentrated at the top.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Cotton introduced the Estate Tax Rate Reduction Act on May 13, 2021.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced.
The bill would have cut the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax rate to 20%, down from the current 40% top rate.
Two Republican senators, Joni Ernst and John Boozman, cosponsored the bill; no Democrats or independents did.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and it received no vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax remains at its current-law rate of 40%, so ordinary taxpayers are spared the unoffset revenue loss, while the wealthiest estates did not get the cut they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers generally; large estates got no cut

industries.note: The bill would have halved the top estate tax rate from 40% to 20%, a large direct transfer to heirs of the largest estates. Because the estate tax applies only above a high exemption, virtually all of the benefit goes to the wealthiest families.
The bill exempts its budgetary effects from PAYGO scorecards, so the lost revenue would not be offset, leaving a larger deficit paid for by the general public.
